title: Introduction to Divide and Conquer
description: Understand how dividing a problem into smaller subproblems makes complex tasks easier

sections.title: 4. Example: Quick Sort Divide Around a Pivot

blocks.text: A fundamental problem-solving strategy. Split a big problem into smaller pieces, solve each piece, then combine the results. You've already seen it in action binary search and merge sort are both divide and conquer.
The idea is simple. Instead of tackling a hard problem all at once
/engineering/dsa-media/1785405851846-266542952.png
The base case is when a subproblem is so small it needs no further splitting  usually when there's only one element left.

Real world analogy: Imagine sorting a giant stack of exam papers. You split the stack in half, give each half to someone else to sort, then merge the two sorted halves together. That's divide and conquer.
Every divide and conquer algorithm produces a tree of calls. The original problem sits at the root. It splits into subproblems, which split again, all the way down to base cases at the leaves.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785405851846-707478232.png
Single elements can't be split further that's the base case. From here, results get merged back up the tree into the final sorted array.
Merge sort is the purest divide and conquer algorithm. Split the array in half until you have single elements, then merge them back together in sorted order.
The merge step how two sorted halves become one
Left: [1, 3, 5, 8]   Right: [2, 4, 6, 7]
compare 1 vs 2 →1 is smaller → take 1
compare 3 vs 2 →2 is smaller → take 2
compare 3 vs 4 →3 is smaller → take 3
compare 3 vs 4 →3 is smaller → take 3
compare 5 vs 6 → 5 is smaller → take 5
compare 8 vs 6 → 6 is smaller → take 6
compare 8 vs 6 → 6 is smaller → take 6
right half finished → take remaining 8
merged result fully sorted!

content.title: 4. Example: Quick Sort Divide Around a Pivot

blocks.text: Quick sort picks a pivot element, then rearranges the array so everything smaller than the pivot goes left, everything larger goes right. Then recursively sorts each side.
pivot = 4 (index 4)
after partition → left of 4: all smaller  | right of 4: all larger → recurse both sides
Time Complexity
Both merge sort and quick sort produce a recurrence of the same shape: split into 2 halves, do O(n) work per level.

T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)
There are log n levels in the tree. Each level does O(n) total work.
Total = O(n) × log n =O(n log n)

blocks.text: Quick sort worst case: Happens when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element the tree becomes unbalanced. Solved by picking a random pivot or using the median-of-three method.

blocks.text: The bigger idea: Divide and conquer is not just a sorting trick. Any time a problem can be broken into independent subproblems of the same shape and their results combined divide and conquer applies.
